prompt: The client asks: "Should we raise the premium plan from $20 to $24 a month?" Fact sheet: the plan has 50,000 subscribers; in a survey, 8% said they would cancel at $24; competitors charge $22–28; monthly churn is 2%; premium sign-ups doubled after a TV campaign last spring.
flawed_answer: Even if 8% of subscribers cancel, revenue rises about 10% to $1.1M a month, and $24 is within rivals' $22–28. The price should go up.
right_parts: the revenue math (about 10% more, $1.1M a month) and the rivals' $22–28 range
model_repair: Raise the price to $24. Even if 8% of subscribers cancel, revenue rises about 10%, to $1.1M a month, and $24 is within rivals' $22–28.

prompt: The client asks: "Should we close our least profitable store?" Fact sheet: the store loses $200k a year; breaking its lease costs $500k; about 30% of its customers would shift to nearby stores, adding $150k of profit; the store is the chain's first location.
flawed_answer: Closing saves the $200k loss but costs $500k to exit the lease. There are good arguments on both sides.
right_parts: the $200k yearly loss and the $500k cost of breaking the lease
model_repair: Close the store. It loses $200k a year, the 30% of customers who shift to nearby stores add $150k, and the $500k lease exit pays back in about 18 months.

prompt: The client asks: "Should our burger restaurants add breakfast?" Fact sheet: adding breakfast costs $20k per restaurant; breakfast would earn about $30k a year per restaurant; the restaurants have been closed in the morning since 2019; the breakfast market grows 5% a year; the chain sells about 2 million burgers a month.
flawed_answer: Add breakfast. We sell about 2 million burgers a month, so customers clearly love the brand.
model_repair: Add breakfast. It costs $20k per restaurant and earns about $30k a year, in morning hours when the restaurants are closed now.

prompt: The client asks: "How should we restore profit at our bakery chain?" Fact sheet: profit fell from $10M to $6M in two years; flour and butter costs are up 35%; menu prices haven't changed since 2023; competitors raised prices 8% on average; store traffic is flat; the chain spent $1.2M on new ovens in 2022.
flawed_answer: Prices might rise about 8% to match competitors, or costs might come down. Each has a case until we know more.
model_repair: Raise menu prices about 8%, like competitors. Flour and butter are up 35% while our prices haven't moved in three years.

prompt: The client asks: "Should the city build a new downtown parking garage or upgrade its existing garages?" Fact sheet: a new garage costs $30M and adds 600 spaces; upgrading existing garages with space-guidance signs costs $6M and cuts the time to find a space 30% for 25,000 drivers a week; downtown visits fell 12% as parking searches got longer; the city already owns the land under its main garage, which cost $1.7M.
flawed_answer: Guidance signs cost $6M and cut search times 30% for 25,000 drivers a week, against $30M for 600 new spaces. Upgrading existing garages should come first.
right_parts: the cost comparison: $6M of signs cutting search times 30% for 25,000 drivers a week, against $30M for 600 spaces
model_repair: Upgrade the existing garages first. For $6M, guidance signs cut search times 30% for 25,000 drivers a week, against $30M for 600 new spaces.

prompt: The client asks: "Should our factory move to 24-hour operation?" Fact sheet: demand is 20% above capacity; a night shift would add 30% capacity and cost $3M a year; serving the extra 20% of demand would add $8M a year in profit before the shift's cost; a new plant would cost $40M; the plant manager has run the factory for 20 years.
flawed_answer: Add a night shift. Serving the 20% of demand we turn away adds $8M of profit for $3M a year, without a $40M plant. Our plant manager has also run the factory for 20 years.
right_parts: the recommendation and the $8M against $3M comparison, without a $40M plant
model_repair: Add a night shift. Serving the 20% of demand we turn away adds $8M of profit for $3M a year, without a $40M plant.

prompt: The client asks: "Should we offer a 20% discount for paying a year up front?" Fact sheet: the monthly plan is $50; the average monthly customer stays 9 months; the annual plan at 20% off would be $480; 40% of surveyed customers would choose the annual plan; in a 2025 test, customers who chose an annual plan had stayed about as long as average; the company has about 12,000 monthly customers.
flawed_answer: Don't offer it. Customers who'd pay $600 a year monthly would pay only $480, a 20% loss.
right_parts: the $480 price of the annual plan
model_repair: Offer the annual plan. The average monthly customer stays 9 months and pays $450, so $480 up front is more, and annual buyers stayed about as long in the past test.

prompt: The client asks: "Should we match a rival's 15% price cut?" Fact sheet: the rival cut prices 15%; we have lost 5% of volume in three months; our margin is 30%; a 15% cut would halve our profit per unit; analysts expect the category to grow 3% next year.
flawed_answer: Matching protects volume and holding protects margin. The right answer becomes clearer after the next quarter.
right_parts: it names the trade-off between volume and margin
model_repair: Hold our price. At a 30% margin, a 15% cut halves profit per unit, so volume would have to double, and we've lost only 5%.

prompt: The client asks: "Should we roll out the loyalty program?" Fact sheet: the program costs $2M a year; in a pilot, 40% of customers joined; members visited 12% more often; annual revenue is $100M at a 25% margin; a rival's loyalty program has 2 million members.
flawed_answer: Roll out the program. 40% of customers joined in the pilot and members visited 12% more often, a big lift in loyalty.
right_parts: the pilot results: 40% of customers joined and members visited 12% more often
model_repair: Redesign the program before any rollout. 40% joined and visited 12% more, but on $100M of revenue at a 25% margin that adds about $1.2M of profit, less than the $2M cost.

prompt: The client asks: "What should we do with our loss-making European division?" Fact sheet: the division lost $20M last year; its revenue has fallen 10% a year since 2023; a buyer has offered $50M; restructuring would cost $80M and might break even in three years; the division is 8% of group revenue; the group bought the division in 2015 for $150M.
flawed_answer: With $20M of losses, revenue down 10% a year and restructuring costing $80M for break-even at best, the $50M offer is better, and $50M at least recovers a third of the $150M we paid in 2015. We should sell.
right_parts: the figures it uses: the $20M loss, revenue falling 10% a year, the $80M cost of restructuring and the $50M offer
model_repair: Sell the division for the $50M offered. It lost $20M last year, revenue falls 10% a year, and restructuring would cost $80M for break-even at best.
